items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: We will concentrate on the three commonly used halogens, but the trend continues for the rest of the group.

items.label: section_header
items.text: REACTING CHLORINE WITH POTASSIUM BROMIDE OR POTASSIUM IODIDE SOLUTIONS

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: Although pure liquid bromine is redbrown, in solution it is orange. If the solution is very dilute it may even look yellow.

items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: You have to be careful with the words you use here. In the exam you must write 'chlorine displaces bromine' not 'chlorine displaces bromide'.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 12.6 Bromine and iodine displaced from potassium bromide and potassium iodide solutions.

items.label: section_header
items.text: DISPLACEMENT REACTIONS INVOLVING THE HALOGENS

items.label: text
items.text: In this section we will look at what happens when we react a solution of a halogen with a solution containing halide ions. These are called displacement reactions - you will see why below. We can use these displacement reactions to show that chlorine is more reactive than bromine, which is more reactive than iodine.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 12.5 Reactivity decreases down the group.

items.label: text
items.text: If you add chlorine solution ('chlorine water') to colourless potassium bromide solution, the solution becomes orange as bromine is formed:

items.label: formula
items.text: 2 KBr ( a q ) + C l _ { 2 } ( a q ) & \quad + \ 2 K C l ( a q ) + B r _ { 2 } ( a q ) \\ \text {potassium} + \text {chlorine} & \quad + \text {potassium} + \text {bromine} \\ \text {bromide} & \quad \text {chloride} \\

items.label: text
items.text: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine and has displaced the bromine from solution. You can think about this in the following way: if something is more reactive, it has a greater tendency to react to form a compound. Something that is less reactive is more likely to go back to being the element (the unreacted form).

items.label: text
items.text: Similarly, adding chlorine solution to potassium iodide solution gives a brown (orange if it is very dilute) solution of iodine.

items.label: formula
items.text: 2 K | ( a q ) + C I _ { 2 } ( a q ) \rightarrow 2 K C I ( a q ) + I _ { 2 } ( a q )

items.label: text
items.text: In exactly the same way, the more reactive bromine displaces the less reactive iodine from potassium iodide solution. Adding bromine solution ('bromine water') to colourless potassium iodide solution gives a brown solution of iodine:

items.label: formula
items.text: 2 K | ( a q ) + B r _ { 2 } ( a q ) \rightarrow 2 K B r ( a q ) + | _ { 2 } ( a q )

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 12.7 Bromine displaces iodine from potassium iodide solution.

items.label: text
items.text: All of the following experiments show no reaction:

items.label: list_item
items.text: bromine + potassium chloride solution: the less reactive bromine cannot displace the more reactive chlorine

items.label: list_item
items.text: iodine + potassium chloride solution: the less reactive iodine cannot displace the more reactive chlorine

items.label: list_item
items.text: iodine + potassium bromide solution: the less reactive iodine cannot displace the more reactive bromine.
